# Distribution calculator {#sec-distribution-calculator}

::: {.callout-tip appearance="minimal"}
This calculator runs **R in your browser**. Nothing is installed on your
computer. The first answer takes a few seconds while R loads.
:::

Choose a distribution, enter its parameters, and choose what to find:

- **density (d)**: the height of the density curve at a value $x$. For a
  continuous distribution this is *not* a probability; it is mostly useful
  for drawing the curve.
- **probability (p)**: the area under the curve to the left (or right) of a
  value $x$. This is the probability that the random variable is at most
  (or at least) $x$.
- **quantile (q)**: the reverse question. Given an area, find the value $x$
  that has that much area to its left (or right).

Below the picture, the calculator shows the R command that produced the
answer. It is the same command you would type in the lab.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof dist = Inputs.select(
  new Map([
    ["Normal", "norm"],
    ["t", "t"],
    ["Chi-squared", "chisq"],
    ["F", "f"],
    ["Exponential", "exp"]
  ]),
  {label: "Distribution"}
)
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof params = {
  const num = (label, value) => Inputs.number({label, value});
  switch (dist) {
    case "norm":
      return Inputs.form({mean: num("Mean μ", 0), sd: num("Standard deviation σ", 1)});
    case "t":
      return Inputs.form({df: num("Degrees of freedom", 10)});
    case "chisq":
      return Inputs.form({df: num("Degrees of freedom", 4)});
    case "f":
      return Inputs.form({
        df1: num("Numerator degrees of freedom", 3),
        df2: num("Denominator degrees of freedom", 20)
      });
    case "exp":
      return Inputs.form({rate: num("Rate (1 / mean)", 1)});
  }
}
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof fn = Inputs.radio(
  new Map([
    ["density (d)", "d"],
    ["probability (p)", "p"],
    ["quantile (q)", "q"]
  ]),
  {label: "Find", value: "p"}
)
viewof tail = Inputs.radio(
  new Map([["area to the left", "left"], ["area to the right", "right"]]),
  {label: "Area", value: "left", disabled: fn === "d"}
)
viewof value = fn === "q"
  ? Inputs.number({label: "Area (between 0 and 1)", value: 0.95})
  : Inputs.number({label: "Value x", value: ["norm", "t"].includes(dist) ? 1.96 : 2})
```

```{webr}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 3.5
#| input:
#|   - dist
#|   - params
#|   - fn
#|   - tail
#|   - value
pars <- lapply(as.list(params), as.numeric)
right <- fn != "d" && tail == "right"
problem <- if (!all(is.finite(c(unlist(pars), value)))) {
  "Please fill in every box with a number."
} else if (any(unlist(pars[names(pars) != "mean"]) <= 0)) {
  "Standard deviations, degrees of freedom, and rates must be positive."
} else if (fn == "q" && (value <= 0 || value >= 1)) {
  "An area must be strictly between 0 and 1."
}

if (!is.null(problem)) {
  cat(problem, "\n")
} else {
  # call the d, p, or q function with the chosen parameters
  call_dist <- function(prefix, v, ...) {
    do.call(paste0(prefix, dist), c(list(v), pars, list(...)))
  }
  tail_arg <- if (right) ", lower.tail = FALSE" else ""
  command <- sprintf("%s%s(%s, %s%s)", fn, dist, format(value),
                     paste(names(pars), "=", unlist(pars), collapse = ", "),
                     tail_arg)
  answer <- eval(parse(text = command))
  x0 <- if (fn == "q") answer else value

  # plotting range: the middle of the distribution, widened to include x0
  lo <- if (dist %in% c("norm", "t")) call_dist("q", 0.0005) else 0
  hi <- call_dist("q", if (dist %in% c("norm", "t")) 0.9995 else 0.995)
  if (dist == "t") {
    # t with few degrees of freedom has very long tails
    lo <- max(lo, -6)
    hi <- min(hi, 6)
  }
  lo <- min(lo, x0)
  hi <- max(hi, x0)
  xs <- seq(lo, hi, length.out = 501)
  ys <- call_dist("d", xs)
  # densities that shoot up near 0 (e.g. chi-squared with 1 df) are clipped
  ytop <- 1.1 * max(ys[is.finite(ys) & call_dist("p", xs) >= 0.02])

  title <- switch(fn,
    d = sprintf("density at x = %s is %s", format(value), format(signif(answer, 4))),
    p = sprintf("P(X %s %s) = %s", if (right) "≥" else "≤", format(value),
                format(signif(answer, 4))),
    q = sprintf("%s of the area is to the %s of x = %s", format(value),
                if (right) "right" else "left", format(signif(answer, 4)))
  )

  par(mar = c(4, 4, 2.5, 1))
  plot(xs, ys, type = "n", ylim = c(0, ytop), xlab = "x", ylab = "density",
       main = title, bty = "l")
  if (fn == "d") {
    segments(x0, 0, x0, answer, col = "firebrick", lwd = 2)
    points(x0, answer, pch = 19, col = "firebrick")
  } else {
    keep <- if (right) xs >= x0 else xs <= x0
    if (right) {
      sx <- c(x0, x0, xs[keep], hi)
      sy <- c(0, min(call_dist("d", x0), ytop), pmin(ys[keep], ytop), 0)
    } else {
      sx <- c(lo, xs[keep], x0, x0)
      sy <- c(0, pmin(ys[keep], ytop), min(call_dist("d", x0), ytop), 0)
    }
    polygon(sx, sy, col = adjustcolor("steelblue", 0.5), border = NA)
  }
  lines(xs, pmin(ys, ytop), lwd = 2)
  abline(h = 0, col = "grey60")

  cat("R command: ", command, "\n", "Answer:    ", format(signif(answer, 4)), "\n",
      sep = "")
}
```

## Things to try

1. For the standard normal distribution (mean 0, standard deviation 1), find
   the area to the left of 1, of 2, and of 3. How do these connect to the
   68-95-99.7 rule in @sec-normal?
2. Find the quantile with area 0.975 to its left. Why does the number 1.96
   keep appearing in statistics?
3. Choose the $t$ distribution and find the quantile with area 0.975 to its
   left for 5, 10, 30, and 100 degrees of freedom. What happens as the
   degrees of freedom grow? (You'll meet the $t$ distribution in
   @sec-confidence-intervals.)
4. Look at the chi-squared distribution with 1, 4, and 10 degrees of
   freedom. How does its shape change? (Chi-squared tests are in
   @sec-chi-square, and the $F$ distribution is used in @sec-anova.)
5. For the exponential distribution with rate 1, compare the probability of
   waiting more than 1 unit with the probability of waiting more than 2.
